title: Two pockets
hookLine: Rabbi Simcha Bunim keeps two notes: "for my sake the world was created" and "I am dust and ashes" (Hasidic tale, drawing on Sanhedrin 37a and Genesis 18:27)

cards: Two slips of paper. That's all today needs. On a bad day a person can feel like nothing: small, useless, invisible.
On another day, the same person can feel like the center of the universe, the smartest one in the room, owed something by everyone.

It's possible to swing between the two in a single afternoon, and to reach for the wrong feeling at the wrong moment. There's a Hasidic teaching for exactly this, told of Rabbi Simcha Bunim, a Hasidic master in Poland.
Every person, he said, should carry two pockets, each with a slip of paper inside.

teach.h: FOR MY SAKE THE WORLD WAS CREATED.
teach.b: In one pocket, a note: for my sake the world was created.
In the other: I am dust and ashes. The teaching is simply this: know which one to reach for. Both lines come from much older sources.

The first is from the Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin. It asks why the Bible tells of one single human being created at the beginning, and answers, in part: to teach that a single life counts as a whole world.

So, it says, each person should say: for my sake the world was created. The second is from Genesis. Abraham is standing before God, bargaining for the city of Sodom, pleading for any good people who might live there.
In the King James words he says he has dared to speak to the Lord, "which am but dust and ashes."
Notice: Abraham says it while he is boldly arguing with God. Humility and courage in the same breath. So when do you reach for which?
When you feel worthless, crushed, sure your life doesn't matter: the first pocket. The world was made for you, too. Your life counts as a whole world.
And when you feel proud, sure you're above someone, about to be cruel because you can: the second. Dust and ashes.
The trick isn't choosing one note forever. It's carrying both, and knowing which the moment needs. Neither is the whole truth alone.

how: Simcha Bunim's two pockets are taught in Jewish schools and sermons, and some people do carry the two notes; the lines come from Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 and Genesis 18:27.

o: holding worth and humility, and knowing which to use
a Sabbath custom of emptying your pockets
keeping one pocket for giving and one for yourself

games.q: which pocket, which source — tap the pairs.
p: for my sake the world was created
reach for the world made for you

s: Abraham called himself dust and ashes while bowing in silence
he said it while arguing with God, pleading for Sodom.
the Mishnah teaches that a single life counts as a whole world
so each person should say: for my sake the world was created.
the teaching says to keep only the humble note
carry both, and reach for the one the moment needs.

games.q: you're about to put someone down because you can. which pocket do you reach for?
o: for my sake the world was created.
games.why: Simcha Bunim's teaching: when pride rises, reach for dust and ashes. when you're crushed, reach for the world made for you.

practice: If you have paper, tear two small slips: on one write, for my sake the world was created, on the other, I am dust and ashes, and put one in each pocket. If you don't have paper, hold one hand, then the other.
Then ask: which pocket does today need?

wordCard.voice: Two pockets. One note says the world was made for you; the other says you are dust and ashes. Reach for the one the moment needs.

orig.note: Hebrew, bishvili nivra ha-olam: for my sake the world was created, from the Mishnah.

carryVoice: Your line: reach for the right pocket. Feeling small, the world; feeling too big, the dust. Sixty days now.

sources.q: which am but dust and ashes
